lessons.title: a Tensor is three fields
lessons.summary: Before the behaviour: the object. Three slots, no array, no shape.

lines: A `Tensor` is a multi-dimensional matrix containing elements of a single data type.
from tinygrad import Tensor, dtypes, nn, Context

claims.text: Tensor inherits RandMixin, not a base class with storage. The frontend is assembled from mixins; the data model is in none of them.
__slots__ names exactly three attributes: uop, is_param, grad. There is nowhere on a Tensor to put an element.

__slots__ also removes the instance __dict__. A Tensor is three pointers. tinygrad creates one Python object per graph node, so this is the difference between a graph that fits in memory and one that does not.

The docstring calls it "a multi-dimensional matrix containing elements of a single data type". No field holds elements. Either they live behind uop, or they do not exist yet — and the second case is the design.

beats.text: This is a Tensor. Before we watch what it does, look at what it is. One class line, one docstring, one line of slots. That is the whole object.
beats.direction: hold on the class line, do not scroll yet

beats.text: uop, is_param, grad. No shape, no strides, no data pointer. If you came from PyTorch you are looking for the array right now, and it is not here.
beats.direction: underline each name with the cursor as you say it

beats.text: Slots is not a micro-optimisation. It removes the instance dictionary. A Tensor is three pointers. This compiler makes one Python object for every node in the graph, so a hundred thousand nodes means a hundred thousand of these — and with a dict on each one, that is a different program.
The docstring calls it a multi-dimensional matrix containing elements. Read the fields again. The elements are behind uop, or they do not exist yet. That second case is the entire design.
So if the Tensor is not the data, where is the data? Next lesson, we follow the constructor to the only thing it can produce.

lessons.title: every constructor ends at a UOp
lessons.summary: Seven input types, five branches, one exit. The type union is documentation; line 90 is the enforcement.

lines: if isinstance(data, pathlib.Path): device = f"DISK:{data.resolve()}"  # keep it on the disk if device is None
_dtype:DType|None = to_dtype(dtype) if dtype is not None else None
# tensors can have gradients if you have called .backward
# create a UOp from the different types of inputs
if _dtype in dtypes.weaks: raise RuntimeError(f"cannot create storage for weak dtype {_dtype}")
data = _fromnp(data.astype(npdtype) if _dtype is not None and (npdtype:=_to_np_dtype(_dtype)) is not None else data)
# by this point, it has to be a UOp
if not isinstance(data, UOp): raise RuntimeError(f"can't create Tensor from {data!r} with type {type(data)}")
# data might be on a different device. NOTE: a const has no device, it doesn't need to look up the default device
self.uop:UOp = data if data.device is None or data.device == (_device:=canonicalize_device(device)) else data.copy_to_device(_device)
# cast on the target device, the source may not hold the dtype (numpy has no fp8/bfloat16) or be able to compute it (DISK)
if _dtype is not None: self.uop = self.uop.cast(_dtype)
# add to all_tensors after construction succeeds

claims.text: Every branch assigns to the same local, `data`, and every branch assigns a UOp. `None`, a Python constant, a numpy scalar, bytes, a list, an ndarray, a Path — seven inputs, one type out.

The last three branches are not convenience. Bytes need a dtype, a list needs one inferred from Python, a Path becomes a DISK: buffer sized by stat().st_size. Three different buffer origins, and the Path one does not read the file.
This is the only gate in the function. The signature advertises seven unions; a wrong object that slips past the branches dies here, not at the type checker.

Two writes follow: move the node to the requested device (skipped when it already is, or when it is a const with no device), then cast. The device lookup is lazy, inside the conditional — a const never pays for it.
The Tensor registers itself with `all_tensors` only after the cast has succeeded. If any branch raised, nothing is half-built and nothing leaks into the scope map.

beats.text: Seven input types, one exit. Watch the bottom of the constructor — that is where the argument is made.
None becomes a constant zero. A number becomes a constant. A numpy scalar becomes a constant. Those three lines never touch memory — there is nothing to allocate yet.
beats.direction: rest on the three const lines

beats.text: Then three that do. Bytes get a dtype and go through frompy. A list or tuple gets a dtype inferred from Python, then frompy again. A Path becomes a DISK buffer, sized from stat dot st size. Notice: the file is not read. Only measured.
Line ninety is the only gate in the whole function. If it is not a UOp by now, raise. The type union in the signature is documentation. This assert is the enforcement.
Two writes follow. Move it to the device you asked for, then cast. And look at where the device lookup happens — inside the conditional. A constant has no device, so it never pays for one.
beats.direction: trace the ternary with the cursor

beats.text: The last two lines are the discipline of the whole file. The Tensor joins all tensors only after construction has succeeded. Nothing is registered twice, nothing is left half-built.
One object in, one UOp out, on every path. Which is why the next stage is allowed to forget that Tensors exist.

lessons.title: a UOp is op, src, arg
lessons.summary: The entire intermediate representation is a dataclass with three fields.

lines: def dtype(self) -> DType: return dtype_from_uop(self.op, self.src, self.arg)

claims.text: Three fields: op, src, arg. op is a member of Ops, a closed enum; src is a tuple of other UOps; arg is anything the op needs. A graph node is these three.
src is a tuple, so a node cannot be edited. You never mutate the graph — you build a new node and let hash-consing collapse the duplicate. Every rewrite is a pure function because of this one choice.
There is no dtype field. dtype is a recursive_property computed from op, src and arg, cached on the node. Store less, derive more — which only works if the derivation is total.

arg is Any. A constant, an axis, a device string, a reduce operation all live in the same untyped hole, and op decides how to read it. It is the one place the IR gives up on types, and it buys a very compact node.

beats.text: A UOp is a dataclass with three fields. That is the entire intermediate representation, and the next three hours are built on it.
op is a member of a closed enum. src is a tuple of other UOps. So a node points down into a DAG, and the DAG is made of nothing but these three fields.
beats.direction: point at src with the cursor

beats.text: src is a tuple, and tuples do not mutate. You never edit a node. You build a new one and let the cache collapse the duplicate. That single choice is why every rewrite in this codebase can be a pure function.
There is no dtype field. dtype is a property computed from op, src and arg, then cached on the node. Store less and derive more — as long as the derivation always terminates.
beats.direction: highlight the decorator, then the body

beats.text: And arg is Any. A constant, an axis, a device name, a reduction. op decides how to read it. It is the one place this IR gives up on types, and it is why the node stays at three fields.

lessons.title: every operation is one line
lessons.summary: There is no add(), no mul(), no relu(). There is one constructor and a parameter.

lines: def alu(self, op, *src:UOp, **kwargs): return UOp(op, src=(self, *src), **kwargs)
def alu(self, op: Ops, *src: Tensor) -> Tensor: return self._apply_uop(lambda *u: u[0].alu(op, *u[1:]), *src)

claims.text: `alu` builds `UOp(op, src=(self, *src))`. Self is operand zero, always. Operand order is positional and load-bearing — CMPNE is not commutative and the scheduler relies on it.
There is no `UOp.add`. The operation is a parameter, so one method serves the whole vocabulary. The compiler's entire elementwise surface is this line plus the enum.
`Tensor.alu` is the same idea one level up: `_apply_uop` unwraps every Tensor argument to a UOp, calls the UOp method, and wraps the result back. The frontend never touches a node directly.
The lambda `u[0].alu(op, *u[1:])` is why Tensor and UOp can share every mixin: the mixin only needs `alu`, `_uop` and `_wrap_uop`, and each type supplies its own.
`**kwargs` is passed straight to the constructor, so a caller can set dtype or arg without a second node. Anything not in the intern key is a silent extra, not an error.

beats.text: You might expect an add method, a multiply method, a relu method. There is one method, and the operation is a parameter.
Self is operand zero, always. Everything else follows in the order you passed it. That order is load-bearing: compare-not-equal is not commutative, and later passes rely on which side is which.
And that is the whole elementwise surface. One constructor, one enum, one line. Adding a new operation to this compiler is adding a member to a list, not writing a method.
Now jump up to Tensor, same idea one level higher. Apply uop unwraps every argument, calls the UOp method, and wraps the result back into a Tensor. The frontend never touches a node.
The lambda is the interesting part. It takes u zero, calls alu on it, and forwards the rest. That is why every mixin in this codebase can be written once and work on both Tensor and UOp.
One caveat: kwargs go straight to the constructor. Pass something the intern key does not name, and nothing complains. The cache is the only gate.

lessons.title: Ops is a closed set, in a load-bearing order
lessons.summary: The enum is the vocabulary, and its declaration order is part of the scheduling semantics.

lines: def _generate_next_value_(_, __, ___, last_values): return 1 + max([0, *last_values, *[max(c) for c in FastEnum.__subclasses__()]])
# the order of these Ops controls the order of the toposort
# this is a RANGE for GPU dimensions, similar to symbolic shapes but not exactly
# BUFFER references bound storage; ALLOC declares unbound global storage

claims.text: `FastEnum` is an IntEnum that keeps Enum's string form and makes `auto()` globally unique across every subclass — the next value is one past the maximum of all values in all subclasses. Two enums cannot share a number.

Global uniqueness is what lets the IR store an op as a small int and still compare enums from different files. It is a compile-time property maintained by a generated counter, not by an explicit numbering.

"The order of these Ops controls the order of the toposort." That comment is a warning: reordering the enum changes traversal order, and traversal order reaches the scheduler. This is not a cosmetic list.
BUFFER is bound storage; ALLOC is unbound global storage. They are adjacent because they are adjacent in meaning, and the comment is the only place that distinction is written down.
This is the complete vocabulary. If an operation is not a member here, the compiler cannot express it — there is no extension point above the enum, only below it.

beats.text: Ops is not in ops dot py. It is here, in the package init, because everything imports it.

Before the enum there is a base class doing something subtle. FastEnum is an IntEnum that keeps Enum's string form, and makes auto unique across every subclass. The next value is one past the maximum of all values in all subclasses.
Why bother? Because the IR stores an op as a small integer, and two enums in different files must not collide. That property is maintained by a counter, not by hand.

Now the comment above the class, which is the most important line in the file. The order of these ops controls the order of the toposort. Reorder this enum and you have changed traversal, and traversal reaches the scheduler.
beats.direction: slow down; this is the point

beats.text: And then the members themselves, each carrying a sentence you cannot get from the name. Buffer is bound storage. Alloc is unbound global storage. Adjacent, because they are adjacent in meaning.
This list is the whole vocabulary. If it is not here, the compiler cannot say it. There is no extension point above this enum, only below it.

lessons.title: the UOp is a singleton
lessons.summary: Fifteen lines that make equality free, and every graph algorithm after them simple.

lines: # NOTE: the key must separate nodes of different dtype: a CONST's dtype is the type of its arg, and True == 1 as dict keys
if (wret:=UOpMetaClass.ucache.get(key:=(op, src, arg, type(arg)), None)) is not None and (ret:=wret()) is not None: return ret
if fret is not True: raise RuntimeError(f"SPEC ISSUE {fret}: {created}")

claims.text: The cache key is (op, src, arg, type(arg)) — four things, no identity. And type(arg) is there because True == 1 as a dict key, so a CONST's dtype would otherwise collide with a different node.
A hit must return a live object. The weakref may have died, so the check is `is not None` twice: the entry exists, and the referent exists. Returning a dead pointer is a crash, not a miss.
A miss stores a weak reference before the constructor returns. Drop every Tensor and the graph frees itself. No global registry, no shutdown step, no leak.
The SPEC block runs only when SPEC > 1, and it runs on the freshly created node. It is a debug validator bolted into the constructor, not part of the semantics.
return created, on both paths. From here on `is` is equality, so the pattern matcher, the scheduler and the linearizer are all allowed to compare nodes by pointer.

beats.text: Everything in this compiler compares nodes. If comparison means walking two trees, every rewrite is quadratic. So tinygrad makes equal nodes identical, and equality becomes a pointer compare.
beats.direction: no highlight yet; frame the problem

beats.text: This runs before any UOp exists. It is a metaclass, so every construction goes through call. It builds a key: op, src, arg, and the type of arg. Four things, no identity.
beats.direction: highlight the class line, then the key

beats.text: Why the type of arg? Because True equals one as a dict key. Without it, a constant storing True and a constant storing one are the same node. The comment says this. It is the kind of bug that would take a day to find.

A hit has to return something alive. The cache holds a weak reference, so the entry can outlive the node. Two checks, not one: the slot exists, and the referent still exists. A dead pointer here is a crash, not a miss.
A miss constructs the node, then stores a weak reference to it. Which means: drop every Tensor and the graph collects itself. There is no registry to clean up and no shutdown path to get wrong.
The SPEC block is a validator, not semantics. It only runs when the flag is above one, and it runs on the node that already exists. Useful, but not part of the story.
And return created on both paths. That is it. Fifteen lines, and every algorithm after this is allowed to be simple.

lessons.title: toposort without recursion
lessons.summary: An explicit stack, a visited flag, and a dict that remembers insertion order.

lines: def toposort(self, gate:Callable|None=None, enter_calls=False) -> dict[UOp, None]:
stack: list[tuple[UOp, bool]] = [(self, False)] # each stack entry is (node, visited_flag)
if gate is None or gate(node):
stack.append((node, True))  # push node back on stack to process after its srcs
for s in reversed(node.src if enter_calls else node.src_without_body):
stack.append((s, False)) # push srcs on the stack
else: cache[node] = None # second time i'm seeing this node, add it to returned toposort

claims.text: The stack holds pairs: the node, and whether its sources have been expanded. It is iterative because a deep graph would blow Python's recursion limit long before it blew memory.
A node is emitted only on its second pop. The first pop pushes it back under its own sources, so it necessarily comes out after all of them.
`in cache` is the whole cost model. Because UOps are hash-consed, this is an identity test against a dict keyed by identity — linear in nodes, not in nodes times depth.
The return type is a dict, not a list. Insertion order is the topological order, so it is a set that remembers when you arrived. Callers get dedup and ordering for free.
src_without_body is what gets walked by default: a call's body is not part of the caller's dependency graph unless enter_calls is set. That is a scheduling decision hidden in one keyword.

beats.text: To rewrite a graph you need its nodes in dependency order. The obvious implementation is recursion. This one is not.
The stack holds pairs. The node, and whether we have already looked inside it. False means not yet. True means yes, and now it may be emitted.
You only come out on the second pop. That is the trick. The node goes back on the stack underneath its own sources, so anything it depends on is guaranteed to be emitted before it.
beats.direction: walk the push/pop with the cursor

beats.text: And look at the guard. If the node is in the cache, skip it. That line costs nothing because of the previous lesson: UOps are hash-consed, so membership is an identity comparison, not a structural one.
The default walk is src without body. A call body is not part of the caller's dependency graph unless you ask for it. One keyword, and it is a scheduling decision.
And it returns a dict, not a list. Insertion order is the topological order. It is a set that remembers when you arrived, which is exactly what every caller needs.

lessons.title: a pass that changes everything and nothing
lessons.summary: transform_to_call rewrites 21 nodes into 21 nodes. A count says it did nothing; +15/−15 says it replaced the graph.

lines: if VIZ: graph_rewrite(big_sink, PatternMatcher([]), name="View Graph")
# The tensor replacement map is collected before these rewrites change node identities.
graph_rewrite(big_sink, pm_callify_ctx_collect, ctx=(ctx:=CallifyCtx()), name="early transform tensor graph")
ret = graph_rewrite(UOp.sink(*ctx.stores), pm_canonicalize_alloc+pm_replace_buf, ctx=ctx, bottom_up=True, name="replace bufs")
if VIZ: graph_rewrite(ret, PatternMatcher([]), name="View Call")

claims.text: Three statements do the work: collect a context, rewrite a new sink from the collected stores, then wrap the result in a call. Two VIZ hooks bookend them and do nothing unless VIZ is on.

The collection happens first on purpose. The comment says the replacement map is gathered before the rewrites change node identity — after that, the map's keys no longer name the nodes they were built from.

The second rewrite does not take `big_sink`. It takes a fresh sink built from `ctx.stores`, bottom-up. The input graph is not edited; it is abandoned, and a new one is assembled from the stores that survived.

`ret.call(*ctx.replacements, precompile=True)` turns the whole tensor program into one CALL node. The graph is not smaller afterwards — it is re-homed, from a pile of stores to a kernel with arguments.

Both VIZ lines rewrite with an empty PatternMatcher, which does nothing but return a graph. They exist so that turning on VIZ shows you the graph at exactly these two moments — before and after the re-homing.

beats.text: This is the pass where the tensor program stops being a pile of stores and becomes a kernel call. Four statements, and the last one is the one to watch.
beats.direction: open on the function, whole body visible

beats.text: First it collects. The comment above the call is the whole reason for the order: the replacement map is gathered before these rewrites change node identities. Build the map after, and every key points at a node that no longer exists.
Then note what the second rewrite is given. Not the big sink. A brand new sink, built from the stores that were collected, walked bottom up. The old graph is not edited. It is abandoned.
And this is why the figure on the right is interesting. Twenty one nodes before, twenty one after. If you only counted, you would say nothing happened. Fifteen in, fifteen out — every node replaced.
beats.direction: let the graph settle; this is the beat the whole lesson exists for

beats.text: A count that is right and a structure that is wrong is the failure a count cannot see. That is not a slogan here. It is this pass.
beats.direction: pause before and after this line

beats.text: The two VIZ lines do nothing — an empty pattern matcher just returns the graph. They are there so that if you run this with VIZ on, you get a picture at exactly the two moments that matter.
